draft.title: Vaccination and immunity
card: A vaccine contains a harmless form of a pathogen, such as a weakened or inactive germ or a part of one. It cannot cause the disease it protects against.
The immune system responds to the vaccine as if it were the real pathogen. It makes antibodies and memory cells, so the body can respond faster if the real pathogen arrives later.
When most people in a community are vaccinated, the pathogen finds it hard to move from person to person. Data show the disease becomes rare.
This also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies, because they are less likely to meet the pathogen. This is called herd immunity.
draft.remember: A vaccine trains the body ahead of time, and when most people are vaccinated, the disease becomes rare for everyone.

a.q: How does a vaccine help the body fight a disease?
opts: It trains the immune system with a harmless pathogen form
It kills the pathogen using chemicals made in the vaccine
It gives the person a mild case of the disease every time
It builds a layer on the skin that keeps pathogens out
a.why: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form of the pathogen, so the body makes antibodies and memory cells before any real infection. It does not give the disease, because the form it contains is harmless.
a.clue: Think about what the body practises on.

b.q: In the town of Wyalong, most people are vaccinated against measles and the disease has become rare. Baby Ari is too young to be vaccinated. Why is Ari still less likely to catch measles?
opts: Measles rarely spreads between people in a vaccinated town
Ari's body makes antibodies from vaccines others received
Vaccines in other people kill measles germs in the air
Ari's skin and mucus block measles better than adults' do
b.why: When most people are vaccinated, the pathogen has few people to spread through, so Ari is less likely to meet it. Ari's own body has not been trained, so it is not Ari's antibodies that give this protection.
b.clue: Ari's protection comes from the people around Ari.

a.best: It trains the immune system with a harmless pathogen form

b.best: Measles rarely spreads between people in a vaccinated town

problems.detail: "It cannot cause the disease it protects against" is too absolute. Live attenuated vaccines (e.g. MMR, varicella, oral polio) can very rarely cause the disease or a mild form of it, especially in people with weak immune systems. Better: "It is very unlikely to cause the disease." Why (a) repeats the claim ("It does not give the disease").

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear answer each. The card states that a vaccine cannot cause the disease it protects against, which is not strictly true for live attenuated vaccines; this should be softened in the card and in Why (a).
